title: Glory on the Mountain, Failure in the Valley
summary: On a high mountain Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James, and John, Moses and Elijah appear with him, and a voice from the cloud calls him the beloved Son. Below, the other disciples have failed to free a boy from a spirit, and Jesus heals him after his father's desperate prayer. Jesus predicts his death a second time, the disciples argue about who is greatest, and he teaches them about childlike greatness, generosity toward other workers, and the seriousness of sin.
story:
Six days after Peter's confession and the first prediction of the cross, three disciples are given a glimpse of the glory that lies beyond it. The transfiguration answers the question the book has been asking, now from heaven itself: this is God's beloved Son. The voice that spoke to Jesus at the baptism (1:11) now speaks to the disciples, and it adds a command, ‘Listen to Him’, which after chapter 8 means listening to what he says about the cross.

The chapter will not let the disciples stay on the mountain. They come down into a crowd, an argument, a suffering child, and their own powerlessness. Then Jesus repeats the prediction of his death as they pass quietly through Galilee (9:31), and they respond by arguing on the road about which of them is greatest. The pattern set in chapter 8 continues: prediction, misunderstanding, teaching. The teaching that closes the chapter, delivered in the house at Capernaum, gathers sayings about the child, the outsider who acts in Jesus' name, the little ones who believe, and the fire of judgment, and it ends with a call to have salt and to be at peace with one another. The disciples keep hearing about glory and missing the road to it; the reader is shown both.
historical:
Mark does not name the mountain, and the question has been debated since antiquity. The earliest identification with Mount Tabor, the isolated dome that rises about 575 meters above the Jezreel Valley in lower Galilee, is attributed to Origen in the third century, and Cyril of Jerusalem names Tabor in his Catechetical Lectures (12.16, around 350). Byzantine and Crusader churches were built on its summit, and the present Franciscan Church of the Transfiguration, designed by Antonio Barluzzi, was completed there in 1924. Many modern scholars favor Mount Hermon, the high massif (about 2,800 meters) that rises above Caesarea Philippi, where chapter 8 was set; others suggest Mount Meron in upper Galilee. The text says only that it was high and that they were alone.

The scribes' teaching that Elijah must come first (verse 11) rests on Malachi 4:5-6, the last words of the prophetic books in the Christian Old Testament (Malachi 3:23-24 in the Hebrew Bible), where God promises to send Elijah before the great and awesome day of the LORD to turn the hearts of fathers and children. Ben Sira, writing in Jerusalem around 180 BC, says Elijah is ready at the appointed time to calm God's wrath, to turn the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob (Sirach 48:10), which is close to Jesus' phrase that Elijah ‘restores all things’ (verse 12). The Mishnah preserves later debates about what Elijah will do when he comes: to settle disputed matters of family status, or, in the sages' view, to make peace in the world (m. Eduyot 8:7), and one saying ends a chain of virtues with the resurrection of the dead coming through Elijah (m. Sotah 9:15). Jesus affirms the expectation and says it has already been met in John the Baptist, to whom they have done ‘whatever they wished’, a reference to his execution by Herod Antipas (6:17-29).

Moses and Elijah were both remembered as men whose departure from this world was unusual. Elijah was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11). Moses died and was buried by God in a grave no one knows (Deuteronomy 34:5-6), and Josephus says a cloud stood over him as he disappeared, adding that Moses wrote of his own death so that no one would say he had gone to God (Antiquities 4.326). Both had met God on a mountain, Sinai or Horeb (Exodus 24; 1 Kings 19).

The word Gehenna (translated hell in verses 43 to 47) is the Greek form of the Hebrew ge hinnom, the Valley of Hinnom on the south and west of Jerusalem, where kings of Judah burned children at the shrine called Topheth (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31-32). Jeremiah said it would be renamed the Valley of Slaughter. In Jewish writings of the centuries before Jesus an accursed valley near Jerusalem became the place of final punishment (1 Enoch 27), and 4 Ezra, written around AD 100, speaks of the furnace of Gehenna (4 Ezra 7:36). The rabbis used the name the same way: the Mishnah says the one who talks too much with women ends by inheriting Gehenna (m. Avot 1:5), and Rabbi Akiva taught that the judgment of the wicked in Gehenna lasts twelve months (m. Eduyot 2:10). The common explanation that Gehenna was the city's perpetually burning rubbish dump is first found in the medieval commentator David Kimchi, around 1200, and has no ancient support.

Exorcism in the name of powerful figures was common. Acts 19:13-16 tells of Jewish exorcists at Ephesus who tried to use the name of Jesus without knowing him, with disastrous results, and the great magical papyrus in Paris (PGM IV, from about the fourth century) includes a spell adjuring a demon by the god of the Hebrews, Jesus. The man John reports (verse 38) was part of that world, and Jesus' answer turns on whether the name is used in faith. Drowning with a weight tied to the neck (verse 42) was a known punishment: Suetonius says Augustus had the tutor and servants of his adopted son Gaius thrown into a river with heavy weights around their necks for abusing their positions (Augustus 67).
cultural:
The shelters Peter wants to build (skēnai, verse 5) are the booths of the Feast of Tabernacles, the autumn festival when Israel lived in temporary huts to remember the wilderness years (Leviticus 23:42-43) and looked ahead to the day when all nations would come up to worship the King (Zechariah 14:16). Peter may be trying to make the glorious moment permanent, or to honor Jesus, Moses, and Elijah as equals; either way Mark says he did not know what to say. The same word, skēnē, is used in the Greek Old Testament for the tabernacle, the tent where God's glory dwelt among Israel.

The cloud recalls the cloud of God's presence that led Israel through the wilderness (Exodus 13:21), covered Mount Sinai, and filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34-35). The note of time, ‘after six days’ (verse 2), is unusually precise for Mark, and many readers connect it with Exodus 24:16, where “For six days the cloud covered it, and on the seventh day the LORD called to Moses from within the cloud.” Moses' face shone after he spoke with God (Exodus 34:29-35); here Jesus' garments become ‘radiantly white’, whiter than any launderer could bleach them. A launderer or fuller (gnapheus) cleaned and whitened new cloth by treading it in water with alkaline earths, a trade carried on outside towns because of the smell; Mark's homely comparison stresses that the whiteness is not of this world. In Daniel's vision the Ancient of Days wears clothing “white as snow” (Daniel 7:9), and white garments mark heavenly beings throughout Jewish apocalyptic writing and in Mark's own empty tomb (16:5). Peter addresses Jesus as ‘Rabbi’ (verse 5), a respectful title for a teacher, literally ‘my great one’.

The boy's symptoms (loss of speech, seizures, foaming, grinding teeth, rigidity, and falls into fire and water) resemble what ancient writers called the sacred disease and we call epilepsy. The Hippocratic treatise On the Sacred Disease, from about the late fifth century BC, argued that the condition has natural causes like other diseases, and Matthew's parallel says the boy is ‘moonstruck’ (Matthew 17:15), the popular term for seizures. Mark tells the story as a case of possession and has Jesus address the spirit directly, while elsewhere the Gospels distinguish sickness from possession (1:32-34). Ancient people did not always draw the line where modern medicine does, and the Gospels themselves hold both categories.

Children in the Greco-Roman world had little status. They were legal minors under their father's control, valued chiefly for what they would become, and Greek used the same word, pais, for a child and a slave. Jesus takes a child in his arms (the rare verb enankalizomai, used again in 10:16) and says that whoever welcomes such a child in his name welcomes him and the one who sent him. The chain of sending reflects a principle stated in the Mishnah, that a man's agent is as the man himself (m. Berakhot 5:5). The millstone of verse 42 is literally a ‘donkey millstone’ (mylos onikos), the large upper stone of a mill turned by an animal, far heavier than the hand mill of a household.

Salt was used to preserve and season food and was eaten together as a sign of loyalty (Ezra 4:14 speaks of eating the salt of the palace). The law required salt with every grain offering, calling it “the salt of the covenant of your God” (Leviticus 2:13), and a lasting covenant could be called “a permanent covenant of salt” (Numbers 18:19). Salt as pure sodium chloride cannot lose its taste, but the salt gathered around the Dead Sea was mixed with other minerals, and if the salt dissolved out, what remained looked like salt and had none of its savor.
literary:
The chapter moves down a mountain in more than one sense. Verse 1 is a hinge that closes the teaching of chapter 8 and opens the transfiguration. The mountain scene (verses 2 to 8) is followed by a conversation on the descent about resurrection and Elijah (9 to 13), and then by the story of the boy (14 to 29), told at greater length and with more dialogue than almost any healing in Mark. The father's cry, “I do believe; help my unbelief!” (verse 24), is one of the most honest prayers in Scripture, and the scene ends with resurrection language: the boy becomes ‘like a corpse’, many say he is dead, and Jesus takes his hand, raises him (egeirō), and he rises (anistēmi), the verbs of 5:41-42 and of the empty tomb (16:6).

The transfiguration is one of three moments in Mark where Jesus is declared Son of God at a turning point: at the baptism (1:11), on the mountain (9:7), and at the cross, where the centurion says, “Truly this man was the Son of God” (15:39). The same three disciples go with Jesus into Jairus's house (5:37) and into Gethsemane (14:33). Readers have long noticed that the mountain scene and the crucifixion mirror each other: shining garments and garments divided by soldiers (15:24), Moses and Elijah beside Jesus and two bandits beside him (15:27), a bright cloud and darkness at noon (15:33), Elijah present and bystanders who wonder whether Elijah will come (15:35-36), and a voice from heaven and a Roman soldier's confession. Mark names Elijah before Moses (verse 4), perhaps because Elijah is the subject of the conversation that follows.

From verse 30 the scene shifts to teaching in Galilee and at Capernaum. The second passion prediction (verse 31) is the shortest of the three, and its Greek sets the Son of Man (huios tou anthrōpou) against the hands of men (anthrōpōn). It is followed, as in chapter 8, by the disciples' misunderstanding (verses 32 to 34) and by teaching on greatness and service (35 to 37). The rest of the chapter is a series of sayings linked by catchwords, a common way of arranging remembered sayings for teaching and memory: ‘in my name’ joins verses 37 to 41; ‘little ones’ and ‘cause to stumble’ (skandalizō, four times) join verses 42 to 47; ‘fire’ joins verses 48 and 49; and ‘salt’ joins verses 49 and 50. The three warnings of verses 43 to 47 (hand, foot, eye) are built in strict parallel, each with the contrast ‘better for you to enter life (or the kingdom of God)… than to be thrown into hell’, and the last is sealed with the closing words of Isaiah (66:24).

outline.t: Some will see the kingdom come with power
Coming down the mountain: resurrection and Elijah
The boy with an unclean spirit and his father's faith
Who is the greatest: the child in Jesus' arms
The outsider who casts out demons in Jesus' name

doctrines.note: On the mountain the disciples see Jesus' glory: his garments shine, the cloud of God's presence overshadows them, and the Father names him. In Scripture glory is the visible weight of God's presence, which filled the tabernacle and the temple; here it belongs to Jesus himself, briefly unveiled. Second Peter recalls the scene as the moment Christ “received honor and glory from God the Father” (2 Peter 1:17), and the church has read it as a preview of the resurrection and of his coming.

The father's prayer shows that faith is not the absence of doubt but trust that brings its unbelief to Jesus (verse 24). Jesus' reply, “All things are possible to him who believes” (verse 23), turns the father's ‘if You can’ back on the father, and yet the healing comes in answer to a faith that confesses its weakness.

The disciples ask why they could not drive out the spirit, and Jesus answers that this kind comes out only by prayer (verse 29). They had been given authority over unclean spirits (6:7), and the failure suggests they had come to treat it as their own possession. Prayer is dependence on God rather than on one's own power, and Jesus himself looked to heaven before healing (7:34).

Jesus speaks of Gehenna three times, with the words of Isaiah 66:24, and urges drastic action against whatever causes sin. The images of cutting off a hand or plucking out an eye are hyperbole, not instructions for self-harm, but they teach that final judgment is real and that nothing is worth keeping at the cost of entering life. Christians differ on whether the unquenchable fire means endless conscious punishment, final destruction, or a purifying judgment; the chapter presses the seriousness of the warning on all of them.

Greatness in the kingdom means being last of all and servant of all, and welcoming the smallest in Jesus' name (verses 35 to 37). The kingdom also has wider borders than the disciples assumed: whoever is not against us is for us (verse 40), and even a cup of water given to Jesus' people will be rewarded (verse 41). Verse 1 promises that some will see the kingdom come with power.

words.note: Metamorphoō, to be transformed or changed in form; four times in the New Testament (Matthew 17:2; Mark 9:2; Romans 12:2; 2 Corinthians 3:18). BDAG describes it as a change into another form. In the Gospels it names the change in Jesus' appearance on the mountain; Paul uses it for believers being transformed by the renewing of the mind and into the Lord's image ‘from glory to glory’. The passive voice in verse 2 suggests that God is the one who transfigures him. The word does not by itself mean that inner glory shone outward; Mark's description of the garments and the voice from the cloud says that.

Agapētos, beloved; about sixty-one times in the New Testament, three in Mark (1:11; 9:7; 12:6). In the Greek Old Testament it translates the Hebrew for ‘only’ in Genesis 22:2, 12, and 16, where Isaac is Abraham's beloved, only son whom he is asked to offer. In Mark it is used only of Jesus: at the baptism, on the mountain, and in the parable of the tenants, where the owner sends his ‘beloved son’ last and the tenants kill him (12:6). The word ties Jesus' sonship to the path of sacrifice.

Apistia, unbelief or lack of trust; about eleven times in the New Testament, three in Mark (6:6; 9:24; and 16:14 in the longer ending). Jesus laments an unbelieving (apistos) generation in verse 19, and the father confesses his own unbelief and asks for help. At Nazareth unbelief left Jesus amazed and limited what he did there (6:5-6). Mark shows that unbelief can be refused, as in Nazareth, or confessed, as here, and the difference matters.

Skandalizō, to cause to stumble, to trip up, to lead into sin; about twenty-nine times in the New Testament, eight in Mark, four in verses 42 to 47. The noun skandalon meant the trigger of a trap or an obstacle in the path. Jesus uses the verb for leading a believer away from faith (verse 42) and for whatever in one's own life causes one to fall (verses 43 to 47). The same word describes the disciples' falling away at his arrest (14:27) and the offense the cross gives (1 Corinthians 1:23, the noun).

Geenna, Gehenna, from the Hebrew name of the Valley of Hinnom. It occurs twelve times in the New Testament, eleven of them on Jesus' lips in the first three Gospels and once in James (3:6). It names the place of final judgment, distinct from Hades, the realm of the dead. Jesus uses it to warn his own disciples, not only outsiders, and he joins it here to the unquenchable fire and undying worm of Isaiah's last verse.

Diakonos, servant, one who waits on others, especially at table; about twenty-nine times in the New Testament, twice in Mark (9:35; 10:43). The word later came to name an office in the church (deacon, Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:8), but here it is the calling of every disciple. Jesus defines greatness by it, and he describes his own mission with the related verb in 10:45: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve.

Halas, salt; eight times in the New Testament, three of them in verse 50. Together with the verb halizō, to salt (verse 49), it closes the chapter. Salt preserved, seasoned, purified, and sealed covenants (Leviticus 2:13; Numbers 18:19), so the saying ‘everyone will be salted with fire’ has been read in many ways: as the testing and purifying of disciples, as the disciple's life offered like a sacrifice, or as judgment. The command to ‘have salt among yourselves’ joins the image to peace within the community.

Proseuchē, prayer; about thirty-seven times in the New Testament, twice in Mark (9:29; 11:17, where the temple is to be a house of prayer for all nations). The related verb proseuchomai appears about ten times in Mark, often of Jesus praying alone (1:35; 6:46; 14:32-39). Jesus' answer that this kind comes out only by prayer (verse 29) contrasts the disciples' attempt with his own life of dependence on the Father. Later manuscripts add ‘and fasting’ (see the note on the text).

christ:
On the mountain Jesus is revealed as the beloved Son whose glory, usually veiled, belongs to him. The voice repeats the Father's words at the baptism in a new form, “This is My beloved Son. Listen to Him!” (verse 7), gathering three Old Testament threads: the king whom God calls his Son (Psalm 2:7), Isaac the beloved son offered on a mountain (Genesis 22:2, where the Greek has agapētos), and the prophet like Moses of whom Moses said, “You must listen to him” (Deuteronomy 18:15). Moses and Elijah, representing the Law and the Prophets and both men who met God on a mountain, speak with him and then disappear, leaving ‘no one with them except Jesus’ (verse 8). He is the one to be heard, and more than a prophet.

The scene also points forward. Luke says Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about his ‘departure’, literally his exodus, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31), and Mark places the vision between two predictions of the cross. On the way down Jesus forbids the disciples to speak of it ‘until the Son of Man had risen from the dead’ (verse 9), so the glory is a preview of the resurrection. Second Peter appeals to it as eyewitness evidence of ‘the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ’ (2 Peter 1:16), and the church has read it as a foretaste of his return and of the glory promised to those united with him (Philippians 3:21).

In the conversation about Elijah Jesus names the Scriptures that shape his own path: ‘it is written that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected’ (verse 12), probably pointing to Isaiah 53:3, where the servant is “despised and rejected by men,” and to the psalms of the suffering righteous. The forerunner has already suffered, and the one he prepared for will suffer too. In the valley the Son who was just revealed in glory takes a boy who looked like a corpse by the hand and raises him, an enacted picture of his own coming resurrection. The second prediction (verse 31) says plainly that he will be delivered into human hands and killed and will rise.

The teaching at Capernaum shows what his glory means for his followers. He identifies himself with a child, so that to welcome the least is to welcome him and the Father who sent him (verse 37), a claim to be the Father's own envoy. He speaks of those who belong to ‘Christ’ (verse 41), the only time in Mark that Jesus applies the title directly to himself before his trial. And he speaks with the authority of the judge, warning of Gehenna in the words of Isaiah 66:24. The Son of the mountain is the servant of all and the judge of all, and the church confesses both.
interpretation:
Jewish tradition lives with the same texts that frame this chapter. The Mishnah's teachers debated what Elijah would do when he came (m. Eduyot 8:7) and looked to him to bring the resurrection (m. Sotah 9:15), and the custom of setting a cup and opening the door for Elijah at the Passover meal, which developed in the Middle Ages, keeps the expectation alive in Jewish homes. Isaiah 66, whose last verse Jesus quotes in verse 48, is read in the synagogue as the prophetic reading for a Sabbath that falls on the new moon, and by long custom verse 23 is repeated after verse 24 so that the reading does not end on judgment; the Jewish Publication Society's Tanakh prints the repetition. Rabbinic teachers spoke freely of Gehenna, and Rabbi Akiva limited the punishment of the wicked there to twelve months (m. Eduyot 2:10), one of several Jewish views of its duration.

The fathers read the transfiguration as a revelation of Christ's divinity and a preparation for the cross. Origen (Commentary on Matthew, book 12, in the 240s) taught that Jesus appears differently to people according to their capacity, and that those who climb the mountain with him see him in glory. John Chrysostom (Homily 56 on Matthew, around 390) read Jesus' promise that some would not taste death as fulfilled six days later on the mountain. Leo the Great, preaching on the Saturday before the Second Sunday of Lent in 445 (Sermon 51), said the vision was given chiefly to remove the scandal of the cross from the disciples' hearts and to show the church the glory its members would share. Cyril of Jerusalem and later pilgrims placed the event on Tabor. The apse mosaic of the Transfiguration in the church of Saint Catherine's Monastery at Sinai, made between about 550 and 565, is among the oldest surviving images of the scene. In the Byzantine church the feast was kept on August 6, and in the fourteenth century the light of Tabor became the center of the hesychast controversy: Gregory Palamas, in his Triads (around 1338), argued that the disciples saw the uncreated light of God's energies, and councils at Constantinople in 1341, 1347, and 1351 upheld his teaching. In the West the feast was made universal by Pope Callixtus III in 1457, after news of the relief of Belgrade from the Ottoman siege reached Rome on August 6, 1456.

Augustine (City of God 21.9) weighed whether the undying worm and unquenchable fire of verse 48 should be taken bodily or of the soul's anguish, and concluded that the fire at least was real, leaving the worm open to either reading. The debate over the nature and duration of hell has continued ever since, with defenders of endless punishment, of final destruction (Edward Fudge, The Fire That Consumes, 1982; John Stott, in Evangelical Essentials, 1988, cautiously), and of universal restoration (David Bentley Hart, That All Shall Be Saved, 2019) all appealing to this passage. In modern criticism Rudolf Bultmann argued that the transfiguration was originally a resurrection appearance placed back into Jesus' ministry, and Robert Stein (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1976) answered that its form differs from every resurrection account. C. H. Dodd (The Parables of the Kingdom, 1935) read verse 1 as saying some would see that the kingdom had already come with power, a keystone of his realized eschatology, while Albert Schweitzer's reading of such sayings as failed predictions of the end was taken up by the philosopher Bertrand Russell, who in his 1927 lecture Why I Am Not a Christian cited the parallel in Matthew as proof that Jesus was mistaken.

In art the most famous treatment of this chapter is Raphael's Transfiguration (1516 to 1520), commissioned by Cardinal Giulio de' Medici and finished after Raphael's death by his pupil Giulio Romano; it sets Christ rising in light above the mountain and, below, the disciples failing to heal the convulsed boy, so that one canvas holds both halves of the chapter. It hangs in the Vatican Pinacoteca. Fra Angelico painted the transfiguration in a friar's cell at San Marco in Florence around 1440 to 1442. In the Revised Common Lectionary, Mark 9:2-9 is read in Year B on Transfiguration Sunday and as an alternative on the Second Sunday in Lent, Mark 9:30-37 on Proper 20, and Mark 9:38-50 on Proper 21; the Roman lectionary reads 9:2-10 on the Second Sunday of Lent in Year B, 9:30-37 on the Twenty-Fifth Sunday in Ordinary Time, and 9:38-43, 45, 47-48 on the Twenty-Sixth. The father's cry in verse 24 has become one of the church's most repeated short prayers.
text:
This chapter has more visible differences between English Bibles than most.

Verses 44 and 46: the words ‘where their worm does not die, and the fire is not quenched’, repeating verse 48, are absent from Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, and other early witnesses, and critical editions omit them. They appear in most later manuscripts and in the King James Version, and were probably added so that each of the three warnings would end the same way. The BSB leaves both verse numbers empty. Some later manuscripts also add ‘into the unquenchable fire’ at the end of verse 45.

Verse 29: most later manuscripts add ‘and fasting’, which the KJV translates. The words are absent from the original hand of Sinaiticus and from Vaticanus, and most editors think they were added as the church placed growing emphasis on fasting; Matthew 17:21, which contains the same saying, is itself absent from the best manuscripts of Matthew.

Verses 23 and 24: later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read ‘If thou canst believe, all things are possible to him that believeth’ and have the father cry out ‘with tears’ and address Jesus as ‘Lord’. The shorter and harder text of Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, in which Jesus repeats the father's own words back to him (‘If You can?’), is almost certainly original.

Verse 49: many later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add ‘and every sacrifice shall be salted with salt’, drawn from Leviticus 2:13, and Codex Bezae has only that clause in place of Mark's. The addition shows that early copyists already read the saying in light of the sacrificial law.

Verse 38: the manuscripts differ in the order and number of clauses in John's report, and the Byzantine text adds ‘who does not follow us’ twice; the sense is unchanged.

Verse 1 concludes the teaching of 8:34-38 as much as it introduces the transfiguration; Matthew and Luke both attach it to the preceding sayings (Matthew 16:28; Luke 9:27). Versification: the promise of Elijah's coming, Malachi 4:5-6 in English Bibles, is Malachi 3:23-24 in the Hebrew Bible.

teach.big: The Jesus who is revealed in glory on the mountain is the Son who goes down to suffer, and those who listen to him learn that his power works through prayer and faith that confesses its weakness, and that greatness in his kingdom means serving the least.

outline.t: Jesus' promise that some will see the kingdom come with power assures his followers that the road of the cross does not end in defeat.
The glory hidden in Jesus is briefly unveiled, and the Father's word to us is simple: listen to him, above Moses and Elijah and every other voice.
Glory and suffering belong together: the forerunner suffered, the Son of Man must suffer, and the resurrection is the key to understanding both.
When disciples fail, Jesus does not; he meets honest, mixed faith with compassion, and his power comes through dependent prayer, not borrowed technique.
Jesus tells his followers the plain truth about his death and rising, even when they are afraid to ask what it means.
The kingdom reverses rank: to be first is to be last and servant of all, and to welcome a child in Jesus' name is to welcome God.
Jesus' people are to rejoice in good done in his name outside their own circle and to value even the smallest kindness done for his sake.
Sin is serious enough to demand drastic measures, especially sin that harms the vulnerable, and a community seasoned by God's purifying work lives at peace.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first treats the transfiguration as a model for spiritual experience, a ‘mountaintop moment’ to be sought and prolonged. Mark tells it as a revelation of who Jesus is, and Peter's wish to stay is gently set aside; the chapter moves at once into the valley of human need. A second preaches verse 23 as a promise that anything can be obtained by enough faith. Jesus is answering the father's ‘if You can’; the point is the ability of God, not the power of the believer's certainty, and the father's weak faith is answered. A third makes verse 29 into a technique, as if certain spirits require a special prayer formula, or, following the added words, fasting as a method. The saying is about dependence on God.

A fourth misreading takes verses 43 to 47 literally. The church has always read them as hyperbole: the Council of Nicaea (325) forbade clergy who had mutilated themselves, and self-harm is never what Jesus commands. The point is that no attachment is worth losing life with God. A fifth uses verse 40 to erase every difference between churches or to claim that anyone doing good is a Christian; Jesus speaks of someone acting in his name, and elsewhere he says, from the other side, that whoever is not with him is against him (Matthew 12:30). Both sayings are true in their contexts. Finally, avoid sentimentalizing the child in verses 36 and 37. Jesus is not praising children's innocence but welcoming the one with no status, and he calls his followers to do the same.
teach.pastoral: The healing of the boy speaks to parents of children with epilepsy, mental illness, or disabilities, and it must be taught with care. Mark presents this boy's condition as possession, but teachers should never suggest that epilepsy or mental illness is demonic, a misreading that has caused great harm; Matthew's own parallel uses the ordinary word for seizures, and the Gospels distinguish sickness from possession. The father's long suffering, ‘from childhood’ (verse 21), and his cry of mixed faith will speak to anyone who has prayed for years for a child. Verses 42 to 48 press on two groups. Survivors of abuse, especially abuse in churches, will hear Jesus' fierce warning against those who cause little ones to stumble, and they should hear it as his taking their side. People prone to scrupulosity or self-harm may hear the commands to cut off a hand or tear out an eye with dangerous literalness; teachers should say plainly that Jesus is using hyperbole and never commands anyone to harm their body, and should keep help visible for anyone struggling with thoughts of self-harm. Those who doubt will find in verse 24 a prayer they are allowed to pray.

hard.q: What did Jesus mean when he said some standing there would not die before seeing the kingdom of God come with power?
hard.a:
The objection is that verse 1, read with the saying just before it about the Son of Man coming in his Father's glory (8:38), predicts the end of the age within the lifetime of Jesus' hearers, and that the prediction failed. Albert Schweitzer (The Quest of the Historical Jesus, 1906) made such sayings the center of his portrait of Jesus as a prophet of the imminent end who was mistaken about its timing, and Bertrand Russell, in his 1927 lecture Why I Am Not a Christian, cited Matthew's form of the saying, which speaks of seeing the Son of Man coming in his kingdom (Matthew 16:28), as evidence that Jesus was wrong and so not as wise as Christians claim. Many critical scholars hold that the saying reflects early Christian expectation of an imminent return, preserved even after it went unfulfilled.

Responses take several forms, and they are not exclusive. Mark himself places the saying immediately before the transfiguration, dated ‘after six days’, and many interpreters from Origen and Chrysostom onward read the transfiguration as its fulfillment: within days, three of those standing there saw the kingdom's glory displayed in Jesus, and 2 Peter 1:16-18 treats the event as a sight of Christ's coming power. Others see the saying fulfilled in the resurrection and the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost, when the kingdom came with power in a way the disciples witnessed; C. H. Dodd (1935) read the perfect tense, ‘come with power’, as meaning that they would see that it had already come. Some link it to the destruction of the temple in AD 70, within the lifetime of many of Jesus' hearers, as a visible act of judgment and vindication. Defenders of these readings add that Mark 13:32 shows Jesus refusing to fix the date of the end. Christians hold these views side by side; what the chapter itself makes clear is that Mark wanted readers to see the transfiguration as a pledge of the kingdom's power.

hard.q: How can a loving God threaten anyone with Gehenna, where the fire is never quenched?
hard.a:
The objection is moral. Bertrand Russell, in the same 1927 lecture, said he could not see how anyone profoundly humane could believe in everlasting punishment, and he counted Jesus' teaching on hellfire as a serious defect in his moral character. Many modern readers, believing and unbelieving, find the image of an undying worm and unquenchable fire incompatible with the love of God that Jesus proclaims elsewhere, and some Jewish readers point out that the rabbis themselves often limited the punishment of Gehenna, as Rabbi Akiva did to twelve months (m. Eduyot 2:10), and that the synagogue repeats Isaiah 66:23 after verse 24 so as not to end on judgment. The objection gains force from how the passage has been used: to frighten children and control congregations.

Christians answer in more than one way, and the question of the nature and duration of hell is one on which faithful interpreters differ. Defenders of the church's majority tradition, from Augustine (City of God 21) to modern theologians such as Robert Peterson, argue that the unquenchable fire and undying worm teach endless conscious punishment, and that the seriousness of the warning measures the seriousness of sin against an infinitely holy God. Those who hold conditional immortality or annihilation, including Edward Fudge (1982) and, tentatively, John Stott (1988), argue that in Isaiah 66:24 the fire and worm consume corpses, so the images mean final and irreversible destruction rather than endless torment. Christian universalists, such as David Bentley Hart (2019), read the fire as the purifying presence of God that finally restores all, and point to verse 49, ‘everyone will be salted with fire’. All three agree on what the passage plainly does: Jesus warns his own disciples, not outsiders, that sin is deadly and that judgment is real, and he speaks in the same breath as the one who welcomes children and promises reward for a cup of water. The warning is given so that no one need go there.

observe: Compare the Father's words in verse 7 with his words at the baptism (1:11). What is the same, what is different, and to whom is each spoken?
Trace the conversation between Jesus and the boy's father in verses 21 to 24. How does each respond to the other's words?
What catchwords link the sayings in verses 37 to 50?
interpret: Why do Moses and Elijah appear with Jesus, and why does the scene end with ‘no one with them except Jesus’?
Why do you think the disciples could not drive out the spirit, and what does Jesus' answer about prayer suggest?
How can Jesus say both that the disciples must welcome a little child and that they must cut off a hand that causes them to sin? How do the two teachings fit together?
apply: The father prayed, “I do believe; help my unbelief!” What unbelief would you need to bring honestly to Jesus if you prayed that prayer today?
The disciples argued about greatness right after hearing Jesus predict his death. Where do you notice yourself measuring rank or importance, even in church?
John wanted to stop someone who was doing good in Jesus' name but was not one of them. How do you respond to Christians outside your own circle or tradition?
